title: The Nervous System and Senses

standard_text: The human nervous system: the central and peripheral nervous systems; the structure and function of neurons; synapses; the reflex arc; the structure and functions of the brain; the human eye (accommodation, pupillary reflex, binocular vision) and ear (hearing and balance); disorders of the eye and ear. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 3; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 3 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): neurons and impulses, synapses and reflexes, the brain and the nervous system, the eye and the ear and nerve impulses and synapses. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A reflex is a fast, automatic response.
key_sub: Receptor → sensory neuron → interneuron → motor neuron → effector.
body_html:
How to think about it

The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the nerves. Neurons carry impulses: sensory neurons from receptors, motor neurons to effectors (muscles and glands). Impulses cross synapses using chemical neurotransmitters. A reflex arc gives a quick response without thinking.

The cerebrum controls thought and voluntary actions, the cerebellum controls balance and coordination, and the medulla oblongata controls breathing and heart rate. In the eye, the lens changes shape to focus (accommodation) and the iris controls the size of the pupil. In the ear, the cochlea detects sound and the semicircular canals detect movement for balance.

Example

Which part of the brain controls balance?

Little brain

Answer: the cerebellum

Example

In bright light, what does the pupil do?

Protect the retina

Answer: it becomes smaller

Common mistakes

  • Thinking reflexes are controlled by the cerebrum.
  • Mixing up sensory and motor neurons.
  • Thinking the lens moves forward and backward to focus.

items.q: Is raising your hand to answer a question a reflex action or a voluntary action?
items.e: Reflexes are rapid, automatic and do not need conscious thought; voluntary actions are controlled by the brain consciously.

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For nervous control, what is the duration of effect?

items.q: What is a Pacinian corpuscle?

items.q: Which part of the sarcomere gets shorter during muscle contraction?

items.q: What causes depolarisation in an action potential?
c: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ ions diffuse in
K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves

items.q: Where is the cardiovascular control centre?

items.q: What is the role of the refractory period?
c: it makes impulses travel in one direction and limits their frequency
items.e: Na⁺ channels cannot reopen straight away.

items.q: What is the resting potential of a typical neurone?
items.e: The inside is negative compared with the outside.

items.q: What causes repolarisation?
c: Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ diffuses out
items.e: The potential falls back towards rest.

items.q: What is a reflex arc?
c: a synapse in the brain only
a pathway from receptor to sensory, relay and motor neurone to an effector
items.e: Reflexes are rapid and protective.

items.q: What is a generator potential?
c: a depolarisation of a receptor membrane caused by a stimulus
items.e: If it reaches threshold, an action potential follows.
